I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I have failed in my most important role in life

issues.explanation: Pregnancy/childbirth/babies as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. No memory, threat, or appraisal item links the trauma to pregnancy, childbirth, babies, parenting, or reproductive themes, so this trigger appears clinically disconnected rather than part of a coherent trigger network.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is also weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The trauma type is childhood physical abuse by a caregiver, but no other selected item suggests medical trauma, injury treatment, bodily examination, or healthcare-related reminders. Given the very specific medical cue content, it does not fit well with the otherwise interpersonal/authority-focused profile.

vignette:
Layla, a forty-three-year-old pharmacist, described her life as a carefully constructed glass house that had begun to show cracks from the inside. For two decades, the precise, orderly world of the pharmacy had been her sanctuary—a place of quiet control and purpose. Now, it was the epicenter of her terror. The precipitating event for seeking therapy was a near-miss medication error, a mistake she caught at the final check, but the tremor in her hands had not subsided for hours. She had come to believe she was a danger to her patients, a failure in the one role that had always given her a sense of worth.

The root of this terror was not in the pharmacy, but in the cold, damp basement of her childhood home. Her uncle, who was her primary caregiver for several years, would lock her there. The memories of this time did not feel like memories at all; they were visceral re-livings. When they came, she was a small child again, the rough concrete pressing into her knees, the air thick with the sweet, acrid smell of his whiskey. The memory that returned most often was not of a specific blow, but of the waiting. He would stand over her, his shadow immense, issuing a string of quiet, nonsensical commands: “Don’t move. Don’t breathe. Look at the wall.” Any deviation resulted in a swift, sharp punishment. The memory felt more real to her than the conversation she’d had with her husband that morning. The feeling of the cold floor, the scent of alcohol, the paralyzing fear of failing to follow an order—it was all immediate, overwhelming her senses until she had to dig her nails into her arm, the sharp pain a desperate anchor to the present. At other times, she could think of these events with a strange, hollow detachment, as if she were reviewing a case study about someone else.

These fragments of the past bled into her present, making her workplace unbearable. The clinical smell of rubbing alcohol used to clean the counters now caught in her throat, instantly transporting her back to the basement. When a doctor called in a prescription, the act of receiving instructions—an order—would cause a surge of panic, making it nearly impossible to focus on the dosage and sig codes. Her concentration, once her greatest asset, was now shattered. She would re-read a single label a dozen times, the words blurring, certain she was about to make a catastrophic error. Every chime of the pharmacy’s entrance bell was a potential threat, and she would flinch, her body tensing for an impact that never came. She had started avoiding her pharmacy manager entirely, communicating through notes and emails to circumvent the anxiety of a face-to-face command.

At home, the life she had built with her husband felt distant and meaningless. He would suggest a dinner out or a weekend trip, and a wall of dread would rise within her. The possibility of happiness felt dangerous, a setup for a future, inevitable catastrophe. She had come to believe that she was fundamentally helpless, that bad things were destined to happen and any attempt to feel joy was a fool’s errand. She would lie awake for hours each night, her body rigid, listening to the house settle, convinced that to fall asleep was to let her guard down. Her husband saw only her withdrawal, her rejection of the life they had shared. For Layla, she was failing him, just as she was failing her patients. The weight of this perceived failure was crushing, confirming her deepest fear: that she could not protect anyone, least of all herself, from harm. She came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified of losing the job and the marriage that were the last vestiges of the competent, meaningful life she no longer felt she deserved.
